title: Speech at work
hookLine: right speech in meetings and messages
tomorrow: what does a boss owe you, and what do you owe back?

cards: A message that starts per my last email can be heard from across the office. Tone travels, even in text. A thumbs-up can read as fine, or as furious.
So how do you put a hard thing kindly? A short sutta gives a five-part test for speech that's well spoken, and it fits on a sticky note. Spoken at the right time.
And said with a mind of goodwill.

teach.b: In Pali, the word for it is subhasita: well spoken. Now notice how much of that list is sound, not content. Two of the five are about what you say: is it true, does it help.

teach.h: TWO ARE WHAT; THREE ARE HOW.
teach.b: The other three are about how it lands: when, how gently, from what heart. A true thing said at the wrong moment, or barked, or sent to win, fails the test even if every word is accurate.
Elsewhere the Buddha describes his own speech the same way.

teach.h: TRUE, EVEN UNWELCOME, AT THE RIGHT TIME.
teach.b: He says what is true and beneficial, even when it's unwelcome, but he knows the right time to say it. So a hard message at work isn't a choice between honest and kind. It's both, tuned.
Say the true thing. Say it when the other person can take it in, not at eleven at night. Use the softest words that are still clear.
Make sure it helps the work, not just your mood. Check the heart it comes from.
And here's the part for the ears: read it out loud before you send it.
Your ear catches what your eyes skip. The edge in as I already said. The chill in a one-word fine.
If it sounds like a slammed door, it reads like one.

how: Right speech is a factor of the eightfold path, and Buddhist teachers offer the five factors of well-spoken speech as a check before speaking or writing.

o: small talk to keep your coworkers happy
saying only what the boss wants to hear
timely, true, gentle words, even hard ones

games.q: the five-part test — tap the pairs.
p: when it can be taken in
the softest words that are still clear

s: if what you say is true, how you say it doesn't matter
three of the five factors are about how it lands: the time, the gentleness, the goodwill.
the Buddha says he speaks true, helpful things even when they're unwelcome
and he knows the right time to say them.
kind speech at work means avoiding hard topics
well-spoken speech can carry hard news: true, timely, gentle.

games.q: a coworker's part of the project has mistakes, it's due tomorrow, and it's 11 p.m. what fits well-spoken speech?
o: message first thing tomorrow: what you found, gently, and how to fix it.
send it now while it's fresh, and blunt, so they can't miss it.
fix it yourself and say nothing, so nobody's feelings get hurt.
games.why: true and helpful, at a time it can be heard, gently and with goodwill: all five. silence skips the truth; blunt at midnight skips the rest.

practice: Think of one true, kind message you could send someone you work or study with: a thanks, a heads-up, a clear no. Type it, then read it aloud, quietly, and listen. Soften one word if it needs it, and send it if it's ready.

wordCard.voice: Speech at work: words that are timely, true, gentle, helpful and said with goodwill, even when the news is hard.

orig.note: Pali: subhasita, well spoken; AN 5.198 names the five factors of speech that is well spoken.

carryVoice: Your line: kind at work. True, and in a voice someone can take in. Four of fifty.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 5.198, Vaca Sutta (speech with five factors is well spoken: at the right time, true, gentle, beneficial, with a mind of goodwill)
Majjhima Nikaya 58, Abhayarajakumara Sutta (the Buddha speaks what is true and beneficial, even if unwelcome, knowing the right time)
